Before writing a project brief, think about where the reader needs to end up.

Maybe they need to get current on a project, understand an unfamiliar situation, or feel ready to make a decision. Each destination calls for a different kind of document.

That's part of why I built Briefly with different brief formats: https://briefly.garrettsdevdesk.com

A good status update helps someone move from being out of date to being current.

They already know the project, so focus on what's changed since the last update, what matters now, any risks or blockers, and what happens next.

Try reading your next status update with that goal in mind. Would someone finish it knowing where things stand?

An executive brief often has a different job from a weekly project update.

The reader may be unfamiliar with the work and need to understand the bigger picture quickly. Give them the purpose, current situation, important facts, risks, and direction without making them read every supporting document.

Build one with Briefly: https://briefly.garrettsdevdesk.com

A decision brief should help someone move from uncertainty to being ready to choose.

That means making the decision clear, explaining the realistic options, and showing the trade-offs and risks involved.

Before sending one, ask whether the reader has enough information to make a thoughtful choice. If not, what important context is still missing?

Executive summary. Leadership update. Project brief. Decision memo.

The names can get confusing, especially when different organizations use them differently. What's more useful is knowing what the reader needs from the document.

Briefly gives you flexible formats for organizing that information: https://briefly.garrettsdevdesk.com

Sometimes the problem with a work update isn't the quality of your notes. You may simply be unsure what the finished document needs to accomplish.

Before writing, ask where the reader is starting and what they should understand or be able to do afterward.

Have you ever rewritten the same information for two different audiences?
